problem: No space left on device with free blocks: inode exhaustion
title: Why can an almost-empty tmp directory reject new files?
question: apt cannot create temporary files, yet /tmp contains little data. What resource do you check before buying more disk?
report: Temporary-file creation failed even though the directory looked small.
evidence: The author's follow-up reported 100% inode usage on the root filesystem. /tmp was a directory on that filesystem, not an independent capacity pool.
fix: The author removed enough files to free inodes. The thread does not identify a complete, safe retention policy for the generating application.
outcome: Author-confirmed inode diagnosis and recovery of available inodes; the long-term source of file growth was not established.
lesson: Check the affected mount's blocks and inodes separately. Why: many small files can exhaust metadata capacity before byte capacity. Next: identify the file owner and growth source before choosing retention.
verification: In a disposable filesystem, compare block and inode usage and verify that a harmless new file can be created after bounded cleanup.
prevention: Monitor both resource types and use application-owned retention. Do not recursively wipe /tmp or production logs.
next: Predict which metric rises fastest when a lab creates many tiny files. Explain why deleting one huge file might barely change inode pressure.

problem: exec format error / no matching manifest for linux/arm64 / multi-platform --load fails
title: Why does Docker say the entrypoint is missing when the file exists?
environment: April 2023 Windows checkout used to build a Linux container; a related startup failure, not an architecture mismatch
question: The image contains its startup script, but executing the entrypoint fails. How do you distinguish missing file, missing interpreter and wrong file format?
report: Previously working source repositories produced images whose shell entrypoint could not execute.
evidence: The author traced the change to Windows CRLF line endings in the shell script, rather than a missing COPY instruction.
fix: Convert the affected script to LF before rebuilding the image. The author posted this solution and another reader confirmed it helped.
outcome: Author-confirmed solution; do not generalize every entrypoint error to line endings.
lesson: Inspect the actual image's script, shebang, executable permission and interpreter. Why: a visible path can still reference an invalid interpreter. Next: rebuild and test the resulting image, not just the edited checkout.
verification: Run the repaired image in an isolated lab and check its normal startup path and health response.
prevention: Use reviewed Git attributes such as a shell-script-specific LF policy; do not bulk-convert binary files or change global Git settings indiscriminately.
next: Compare two tiny disposable scripts with different line endings, and explain the error before revealing the difference.

problem: After a Docker upgrade every Traefik route vanished: 'client version 1.24 is too old'
title: Why did a Docker upgrade remove every Traefik route?
environment: November 2025 report: Docker 29.0.0 with Traefik 3.6.0; historical version pair
question: All application containers are running, but routing fails immediately after an Engine upgrade. Why inspect the discovery provider before editing every application?
report: Traefik's Docker provider could not retrieve server information after the upgrade.
evidence: The log explicitly rejected client API 1.24 because the daemon required at least 1.44.
fix: Merged Traefik PR #12256 removed the hardcoded API version and enabled client/server API negotiation. Use an official supported release containing the fix, after compatibility testing.
outcome: Upstream fix is evidenced by the linked merged PR, not merely the issue's closed status.
lesson: Correlate the dependency upgrade with provider errors. Why: failed discovery can affect every route at once. Next: test a fixed proxy version before changing application labels.
verification: In staging, verify provider discovery, one route from each deployment mode, and HTTPS behavior with the selected versions.
prevention: Pin compatible versions and canary upgrades. Do not install a stranger's temporary image or lower daemon safeguards merely because a comment suggests it.
next: Write a two-component upgrade matrix and rollback boundary for Docker and Traefik.

problem: Docker-image app goes 404 after a webhook or API redeploy: Traefik labels dropped from the Swarm service (Dokploy #5453)
title: Why is a successful Dokploy redeploy followed by 404s?
environment: September 2026 issue report: Dokploy 0.29.12 and 0.30.6, Docker-image apps on a single-node Swarm
question: CI reports success and the app is healthy, but every hostname returns 404. Which before/after object explains the difference?
report: The reporter observed routing labels disappear from the Swarm service after webhook and API redeploys.
evidence: Current service labels were empty while PreviousSpec retained them; the task itself remained healthy.
fix: The reporter restored labels with a periodic workaround and noted that service rollback also restored them. Rollback can revert the image as well as labels.
outcome: Reported workaround only. No permanent upstream fix is established by the retrieved issue; do not present this as universally solved or as your own confirmed incident.
lesson: Compare desired service specification with the previous version. Why: container health does not prove ingress configuration survived. Next: restore a reviewed known-good specification through the authoritative deployment configuration.
verification: Check every hostname externally, confirm the intended image digest, then repeat a controlled redeploy to test persistence.
prevention: Add post-deploy route smoke tests. Avoid a permanent label-repair loop that races the deployment controller.
next: Draft a lab before/after checklist: labels, image digest, task health, router discovery and external response.

problem: Traefik/Dokploy returns 502 Bad Gateway for a container app
title: A solved Swarm 502 thread: should you really rebuild the cluster?
environment: November 2019 Traefik v2 / Swarm thread, with later replies; historical topology
question: The public proxy responds, but the backend connection reports no route to host. Is changing the HTTP router rule the next useful step?
report: The author narrowed a 502 to Swarm networking after enabling diagnostic logging.
evidence: The backend connection error identified a reachability failure, despite matching network names and IDs.
fix: The author reported recovery after recreating the Swarm and suspected an earlier manager-hostname change.
outcome: Recovery is author-confirmed; the hostname hypothesis was not proven. Broad reconstruction changed too many variables to isolate a root cause.
lesson: Test reachability from the proxy's network context before altering routing rules. Why: a matching router cannot repair an unreachable backend. Next: inspect overlay membership, node connectivity, firewall rules and MTU.
verification: Test replicas on different nodes and repeat after rescheduling in a disposable Swarm.
prevention: Do not copy replies that disable firewalls or force managers out of a production Swarm. Plan disruptive recovery with quorum, service specifications and backups protected.
next: Explain why a successful rebuild proves recovery but not the suspected cause.

problem: Agent shows Never connected or Pending
title: Wazuh: when agent replacement solved a never-connected report
environment: May 2021 Windows 10 and Wazuh 4.0-era discussion; incomplete exact version inventory
question: An agent is registered but remains inactive. What would distinguish version compatibility from a blocked event connection?
report: The agent appeared in the manager after manual key registration but did not become connected.
evidence: Support asked about manager/agent compatibility and connectivity. The author later reported success after uninstalling the old agent and installing a newer one.
fix: Agent replacement was the reported recovery action. The final version pair was not recorded, and the author's version wording does not cleanly establish the support reply's specific incompatibility.
outcome: Author-confirmed recovery, with incomplete root-cause evidence. Older agents are not universally incompatible with newer managers.
lesson: Record both versions and agent logs before re-enrollment. Why: registration alone cannot distinguish protocol compatibility from transport failure. Next: follow the compatibility and enrollment checks for the installed release.
verification: Verify active status and arrival of a benign test event; status alone is not the whole monitoring pipeline.
prevention: Stage compatible upgrades and preserve agent identity/group configuration. Do not blindly reinstall the newest agent on an older manager.
next: Make a two-branch diagnosis for service/version errors versus event-port connection failures.

problem: kubeadm init fails or the control plane keeps restarting: containerd has CRI disabled or the wrong cgroup driver
title: Kubernetes node join failures and mismatched cgroup drivers
environment: 2021–2022 thread: Kubernetes 1.22, Ubuntu 20.04 and the historical Docker/dockershim setup
question: Node join fails and API connections reset. Which local services and logs should you inspect before repeatedly replacing the join token?
report: The original question included connection resets during joining. A later participant reported a similar installation recovered after changing Docker's cgroup driver to systemd.
evidence: The recovery claim is from a later participant, not the original author; the initial log does not by itself prove a driver mismatch.
fix: Align the kubelet and runtime cgroup configuration when evidence shows a mismatch. The historical Docker edit is not a containerd configuration recipe.
outcome: Reply-reported solution for a similar environment; original incident resolution is not confirmed.
lesson: Check kubelet/runtime health and explicit cgroup errors. Why: the API symptom can be downstream of node-service failure. Next: use the installed runtime's current configuration documentation.
verification: In a disposable cluster, verify stable node readiness, pod creation and absence of recurring runtime errors.
prevention: Use consistent node configuration. Changing drivers on joined nodes is disruptive and needs a supported replacement or migration plan.
next: Draw kubeadm → kubelet → runtime, and assign one source of evidence to each boundary.
official_title: Kubernetes container runtimes and cgroup drivers

problem: Adopting existing infrastructure: 'already exists' errors and how to import
title: Terraform multi-region import: why does fixing a provider reveal destruction?
environment: January 2024 Terraform 1.6/1.7 and AWS provider 5.31; imported multi-region configuration
question: Terraform asks for a default provider, but adding one sends resources toward the wrong region. How do you trace the actual provider binding?
report: The author struggled with aliased regional providers while importing existing infrastructure.
evidence: A maintainer explained implicit defaults and module provider mappings. The author then confirmed explicit regional resource bindings resolved the provider issue.
fix: Correct provider associations in configuration. Manual edits to state were not the maintainer's recommended fix.
outcome: Author-confirmed provider correction. Destructive plan changes and externally managed resources remained a separate unresolved concern.
lesson: Inspect terraform providers and each module's mapping. Why: a child module has its own provider namespace. Next: review every planned resource action instead of treating a successful plan as approval to apply.
verification: Confirm target account/region and explain every proposed replacement or deletion before any apply.
prevention: Test reusable module mappings and define ownership boundaries with other controllers; preserve state backups.
next: Trace two regional aliases into child modules on paper, including one deliberately missing mapping.
official_title: Terraform provider inheritance and explicit mappings

problem: Loki queries fail: 'too many outstanding requests', 'maximum of series (500) reached', entry and time-range limits, timeouts
title: Loki is slow: when changing ingestion helped more than tuning knobs
environment: 2024 Loki on Kubernetes with S3 and shared read/write node capacity
question: Queries are slow and logs seem missing. What workload evidence should you gather before raising timeouts and parallelism?
report: The operator shared performance problems and a heavily tuned Loki configuration.
evidence: In the later follow-up, the author reported most performance problems improved after changing ingestion and making log lines smaller.
fix: Reduce unnecessary ingested content and review labels/workload shape. The thread does not prove every missing-log symptom was fixed.
outcome: Author-reported partial improvement, not a complete measured resolution of all symptoms.
lesson: Measure line size, ingestion volume, stream cardinality and read/write contention. Why: raising limits can amplify load. Next: compare a bounded workload before and after one change.
verification: Measure query latency and resource use, then reconcile known test events end to end to detect silent loss.
prevention: Agree retention and field requirements before dropping data. Preserve audit/security evidence; follow Loki's label-cardinality guidance.
next: Design a lab A/B comparison of verbose and minimal synthetic logs with the same event count.

problem: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon in docker-in-docker (2375 vs 2376, TLS, privileged, service name)
title: Why did unchanged GitLab jobs break after a docker:dind update?
environment: July 2019 vendor advisory about Docker 19.03; compare with current runner documentation
question: The pipeline configuration did not change, but the Docker service now rejects the client. What changed outside the repository?
report: GitLab documented CI failures following Docker-in-Docker's move to TLS by default.
evidence: An unpinned service image could upgrade independently; old plaintext connection assumptions no longer matched the daemon.
fix: The TLS-preserving path shares generated client certificates with the job and aligns its connection settings with the TLS endpoint. Current documentation also covers executor-specific alternatives.
outcome: Vendor-documented remediation, not an individual author's verified production outcome. The associated issue body was only available through indexed text; this card relies on the readable advisory.
lesson: Check resolved image versions, daemon logs, hostname, certificate mounts and port together. Why: changing only 2375 to 2376 is insufficient without usable credentials. Next: test daemon access before rebuilding the application.
verification: On an isolated runner, verify docker info and one harmless build using the intended trust configuration.
prevention: Pin reviewed image versions and avoid blanket TLS disabling. Privileged DinD requires dedicated isolation and a separate security decision.
next: Draw job container → TLS connection → DinD service, labeling the certificate-sharing boundary.

problem: The backup job 'succeeded' for weeks but produced empty or unusable files
title: GitLab 2017: what if the backups are not usable during an outage?
environment: 31 January 2017 GitLab.com PostgreSQL incident; historical production postmortem
question: The primary data is damaged, replication is unusable and scheduled backups are missing. How do you choose the least-bad recovery source?
report: GitLab's recovery exposed failures in several backup assumptions after production database data was removed.
evidence: The dump process used an older PostgreSQL client than the server. A manually created LVM snapshot from roughly six hours earlier was available.
fix: The team recovered using the available snapshot/staging data, handled webhook recovery separately, and gradually restored service.
outcome: Service restored with data loss. This is not a zero-loss restore or evidence that replication replaces backups.
lesson: Inventory recovery points and validate contents before committing to a restore. Why: a job schedule is not proof of usable data. Next: estimate loss and restore time explicitly.
verification: Lab acceptance should include records, sequences, application behavior and external side effects—not merely database startup.
prevention: Test restores, client/server compatibility and failure alerts. Keep recovery copies isolated and suppress real webhooks in restore labs.
next: Prepare a tabletop recovery choice between snapshots of different ages and speeds; state the RPO/RTO tradeoff.

problem: Ran the command on the wrong server
title: Resend 2024: a local migration targeted production
environment: 21 February 2024 production outage; published recovery and improvement plan
question: A developer starts a migration locally, but production tables disappear. What do you verify before restoring a backup?
report: The migration used the production connection. The first lengthy restore failed because the wrong backup timestamp had been selected.
evidence: The incident timeline distinguishes completion of the first restore from discovery that the required data had not returned.
fix: An older backup was selected for a second restore; the API and dashboard returned after it completed.
outcome: Service restored after about twelve hours, with a reported five-minute data-loss window. Planned reconstruction was not already completed in the report.
lesson: Verify target identity and a recovery point preceding the destructive change. Why: successful execution can still produce the wrong database. Next: validate restored contents before reopening writes.
verification: Check a known pre-incident record, recent-write boundary, schema and an end-to-end application operation in isolation.
prevention: Separate development credentials and production migration authority; make destructive production changes an explicit reviewed workflow.
next: Write the connection-identity checks and stop conditions you would require before a migration and before a restore.

problem: A routine config change takes production down
title: Cloudflare 2019: how can one WAF rule exhaust CPU worldwide?
environment: 2 July 2019 global edge outage; historical first-party postmortem
question: CPU saturates and 502s rise across many locations after a rules update. How do you distinguish expensive execution from an external traffic attack?
report: A newly deployed WAF regular expression consumed excessive CPU, including while the rule was in simulation mode.
evidence: Live CPU investigation and supporting logs identified WAF processing; ordinary functional tests had not exposed runaway runtime cost.
fix: Responders temporarily terminated WAF execution, validated the rollback in one location, then restored WAF functionality globally.
outcome: Traffic and CPU recovered; security functionality was subsequently re-enabled. The report describes emergency mitigation, not a recommendation to routinely disable protection.
lesson: Correlate a global symptom with a global change and execution cost. Why: non-blocking rule mode still runs code. Next: canary the correction and test both safety and availability.
verification: Check CPU, error rates and expected security behavior together before declaring a lab rollback successful.
prevention: Add bounded performance tests, staged rule deployment and rehearsed emergency access independent of the failing service.
next: Tabletop the approval and compensating-control decisions for a security-affecting emergency mitigation; do not disable your protections.

title: Cloudflare 2022: when a routing-policy change removes reachability
environment: 21 June 2022 BGP policy incident; advanced routing comparison, not a Linux default-gateway recipe
question: A reviewed network change takes 19 locations offline, including normal management access. What makes rollback possible?
report: Reordering routing-policy terms withdrew critical prefixes in locations using a newer network architecture.
evidence: Earlier rollout locations used a different architecture and did not expose the failure. The change also impaired responders' access.
fix: Engineers used backup access procedures and reverted the policy. Overlapping responder changes delayed recovery by undoing some reverts.
outcome: The first location returned at 06:58 UTC and all affected locations were back by 07:42 UTC, according to the report.
lesson: Test representative architecture, not just a small site count. Why: an unrepresentative canary can pass. Next: appoint change ownership and verify actual prefix reachability.
verification: Use independent reachability checks and management-path checks after each staged lab change.
prevention: Keep tested out-of-band access, policy-diff validation and a single coordinated rollback plan.
next: Design a tabletop rollout spanning two architectures and explain where to pause. Do not experiment with public BGP announcements.

problem: HAProxy 503 'No server is available to handle this request': every backend server marked DOWN
title: Slack 2020: why did adding more servers not fix 503s?
environment: 12 May 2020 HAProxy/Consul incident; not a report about every backend being DOWN
question: Only a subset of a large application fleet is overloaded, and scaling adds idle servers. Where might capacity be getting lost?
report: Slack's HAProxy backend state stopped updating after its state-management program ran out of configured server slots.
evidence: The updater tried allocating new slots before freeing obsolete ones. Over time, proxies retained stale backends while instances changed.
fix: A rolling restart of the HAProxy fleet restored current backend state and mitigated the outage.
outcome: First-party reported service recovery. Monitoring for this condition existed but had not worked as intended.
lesson: Compare discovered, configured and actually serving backends. Why: compute capacity is useless if traffic cannot reach it. Next: reconcile control-plane state before adding more workers.
verification: In a lab, check load distribution and backend membership through a scale-up and scale-down cycle, not just one successful request.
prevention: Exercise discovery-limit alerts and churn tests. A proxy restart is a mitigation, not a substitute for repairing reconciliation.
next: Model three backend slots and four instances on paper, then remove an old instance and explain the allocation-order bug.

problem: No tested restore: RTO and RPO discovered during the disaster (and ransomware deleting the backups too)
title: GitHub 2018: why did a short network fault need a long recovery?
environment: 21–22 October 2018 MySQL/Orchestrator incident; related recovery-scale lesson, not an example of entirely untested backups
question: Connectivity returns after 43 seconds, but writes exist in two different regional histories. Why is immediate failback dangerous?
report: Automated failover produced a topology that application latency assumptions could not support; databases had diverging writes.
evidence: Both regions contained writes absent from the other. Safe failback required more than restoring the network link.
fix: GitHub preserved writes, restored and synchronized replicas, recovered a stable topology, then processed queued work.
outcome: Service returned after 24 hours and 11 minutes. The report still described manual reconciliation of some writes; do not erase that qualification.
lesson: Prioritize data integrity and constrain failover to supported topologies. Why: automated election can succeed while the application fails. Next: monitor replication catch-up and backlog independently.
verification: A recovery drill should check consistency, replication lag, latency and queued side effects, not simply primary availability.
prevention: Test full recovery scale and regional partitions. This team tested restores, but had not previously needed this entire-cluster recovery path.
next: Explain a fail-forward decision to a nontechnical stakeholder, including uncertainty in the recovery estimate.
